newsitem.title: SPAIN: POLL - Iberian spread seen to continue steady fall.
newsitem.headline: POLL - Iberian spread seen to continue steady fall.

text.p: Iberian bonds are expected to narrow the yield spread to their 10-year German counterparts steadily, unless there is a delay in the launch of European economic and monetary union, a Reuter poll showed on Monday.

According to a poll conducted last week of 13 experts, the Spanish and Portuguese 10-year spreads are seen falling to 55 basis points by year end, according to the median forecast, or the middle value of the polled forecasts.
This compares with 68 basis points and 70 basis points, respectively, on Monday morning.
The mean predicts higher values -- 78 basis points for Spain and 68 for Portugal -- mainly due to two London firms' prediction of a different trend.
"Our forecasts are based on the idea that there'll be a delay in EMU's start," said Gwyn Hacche, economist at HSBC in London.
"That will be clear from the fourth quarter this year and at that point investors will switch money from Spain, and France and Italy, toward Germany."

He expected the Spanish spread to end 1997 at around 190 basis points, while at London's 4Cast another economist expressed a similar view saying the spread could end the year at around 120 basis points.
But others are more bullish and expect the current downtrend in the spread to continue. The Spanish spread has narrowed from 330 basis points in March 1996 and the Portuguese from 320 points.
"Our forecasts are based on the hypothesis that we will have a timely euro and Spain will be part of it from its start," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
"We'll meet the convergence criteria, maybe better than France and Germany," Fernandez said.

Isabel Cabral, economist at Fincor in Lisbon, expects the Portugal to Germany yield spread to be around 60 basis points at the end of 1997 and then gradually fall toward 15 basis points in the first quarter of 1999.
"Portugal has very good probability to be in the leading group of countries giving life to EMU," she said.

Another economist at a foreign bank in Lisbon said to expect the Portuguese spread to fall toward 50 basis points this year and to around 20 in 1999. And the forecast was based on a "timely EMU, which will include Portugal," he said.

Credit Lyonnais' Fernandez said that given a 100 percent probability of Spain joining Europe's single currency founders "would imply a (10-year spread) at around 50 basis points now. We are not trading at this level because there are still some uncertainties," he said.

"There is the possibility of official remarks which could awake more jitters and move the spread. That explains why the spread is not trading now, and will not trade in coming months, with the certainty of the full convergence," Fernandez added.
Although both Portuguese and Spanish spreads should progressively fall as the entrance of the two in EMU grows more likely, experts' forecast it would never be zero.

"Longer term...the spread would not come to zero, because some risk premium for the country risk is likely to remain, for the rating and the liquidity," said Fernandez, who expects the spread to stay at around 15 basis points for Spain and 20 basis points for Portugal in the second quarter of 1999.
"Once it is in, Portugal will maintain a spread at around 20 basis points," said the economist of the foreign bank in Lisbon.
